parts.label: Part 4
parts.article:
Morning everyone. Welcome back to this series of lectures on the development of photography. Last week we looked at a type of photography called Daguerreotype, the first commercially successful photographic process. Today we're going to look at how this was gradually replaced by a technique called Calotype. Daguerreotype was a major breakthrough but there were problems with it. In particular, because the image was produced on a copper sheet, it was expensive to create each photograph.
As a result during the 1840s a man named William Talbot began looking for an alternative approach. Talbot eventually became an influential figure but he always said he was not a professional photographer. In fact he trained as an artist. His greatest interest was painting and he only became involved with photography as a secondary interest. Talbot spent many years trying to solve the problems associated with Daguerreotype photography. He tried a number of different approaches and it took some time to find a successful alternative but in the end what he did was instead of producing each photograph on a sheet of copper he produced them on paper and at the time this was a great advance. Talbot's technique, which he called Calotype photography, had other advantages as well. Maybe the most important was that the pictures themselves weren't as sharp as the ones produced before. The sharpness had been a problem because it distorted everything but this new Calotype process produced images that were realistic compared to all earlier photographs.
Calotype photography was invented in Britain but it was also popular with French photographers. The 1850s were a time of rapid development in France and photography was used to record these changes. One example of how important photography had become occurred in 1851 when the French government established a society to promote the interests of photographers, something that hadn't happened before. To begin with, there were five members and maybe the most important was a man called Gustave Le Gray. Le Gray became increasingly fascinated by the Calotype process. Most of all he wanted to produce different types of images so began a series of experiments to see how this might be done. His greatest success was when he designed the first camera that was able to create enlargements - an important step forward.
Another of Le Gray's innovations was his work on the size of the equipment necessary to take photographs. Originally it was very heavy and difficult to move about but Le Gray made it lighter and smaller. This meant he could take photographs outdoors more easily rather than being limited to the studio which had sometimes been the case until then. Le Gray produced numerous photographs during this period and was highly regarded among fellow photographers. But his work also became famous among the general public because he wrote a very popular series of books describing the Calotype process and giving examples of his work. The simple fact was that people liked photography. They thought it was reliable, especially compared to drawing where the human hand might alter or exaggerate things.
This had various consequences. One of which was that photography was now often used to record the huge program of renovation work of historical buildings in France during the 1850s. The camera doesn't lie, so people said. As a result, the Calotype process was admired not only by photographers but increasingly by the government and by mainstream society. However, debates still remained about whether photography could truly be called an art form like sculpture or drawing. Certainly, although the public liked it, in the opinion of critics, photography could not be compared to other established forms of art.
So, in summary, what can we say about Calotype photography during this period? One thing to re-emphasize is that the 1850s were a period of great development in Britain and France. The culture in both countries admired all new technological advances and photography represented these ideas because it was considered to be a science by most people. However, photographers didn't stop experimenting with new materials to improve the quality of their work. Most of all, they were searching for ways to make images more permanent because Calotype photographs tended to fade over time. And in the end, they found that if the image was produced on glass, it lasted much longer. So Calotype photography was slowly replaced by other techniques which had greater...

analyses.content: 录音中提到因为图像是在铜片上生成的，所以制作每一张照片都非常昂贵（expensive）。
In particular, because the image was produced on a copper sheet, it was expensive to create each photograph.
题目中已经出现了 “copper”，不需要再填一遍，核心形容词是 expensive。
In fact he trained as an artist. His greatest interest was painting and he only became involved with photography as a secondary interest.
题目已经说了他是 “artist”，所以不要填 artist，要填具体的领域 painting。
录音说 Talbot 最感兴趣的是绘画（painting），虽然题目用了 specialised in，对应录音里的 greatest interest。
The sharpness had been a problem because it distorted everything but this new Calotype process produced images that were realistic compared to all earlier photographs.
你可能会听到 “sharp”，但录音说的是“不如之前的照片清晰”，所以 sharp 是反义干扰，不要填。
录音指出这个新的 Calotype 工艺生成的图像比起之前的照片更加逼真（realistic）。
His greatest success was when he designed the first camera that was able to create enlargements - an important step forward.
“Experiments” 是他做的动作，不是最后生成的产物，不要填错。
录音提到 Le Gray 最大的成功是设计出了第一台能够制作放大照片（enlargements）的相机。
This meant he could take photographs outdoors more easily rather than being limited to the studio which had sometimes been the case until then.
题目是 “outside the...”，虽然录音提到了 “outdoors”，但这里需要填他走出的那个特定地点。
录音说设备变轻便了，意味着他可以更容易地在户外拍照，而不再局限于画室/摄影棚（studio）。
录音说因为他写了一系列非常受欢迎的书（books）来描述这个工艺，所以 Calotype 变得出名了。
But his work also became famous among the general public because he wrote a very popular series of books describing the Calotype process and giving examples of his work.
不要填 “examples” 或 “work”，这些是书里的内容，让工艺出名的是这一系列 books。
One of which was that photography was now often used to record the huge program of renovation work of historical buildings in France during the 1850s.
“Renovation” 是修饰 “work” 的，而且题目空格前是 old，填 renovation 语义不通。
录音提到摄影常被用来记录法国历史建筑（historical buildings）的翻修工作，题目中的 old 对应 historical。
Certainly, although the public liked it, in the opinion of critics, photography could not be compared to other established forms of art.
前面提到了 “public” 喜欢摄影，但认为摄影不是艺术的是 critics，不要张冠李戴。
录音明确说，在评论家（critics）看来，摄影不能和其他既定的艺术形式相提并论。
The culture in both countries admired all new technological advances and photography represented these ideas because it was considered to be a science by most people.
题目中的 “thought of as” 对应录音中的 “considered to be”。
录音提到摄影反映了当时的观念，因为大多数人认为它是一门科学（science）。

Most of all, they were searching for ways to make images more permanent because Calotype photographs tended to fade over time. And in the end, they found that if the image was produced on glass, it lasted much longer.
“Permanent” 是他们寻找的目标（make images more permanent），而实现这个目标的材料是 glass。
录音最后说人们发现如果图像是在玻璃（glass）上生成的，保存时间会长得多。
